opus-5.5.text:
I think it's hard to overstate. If you look at the people actually doing the work at the top AI labs in the U.S., whether that's OpenAI, Google DeepMind, Anthropic, Meta, or the academic groups training open models, a huge share of the researchers were born in China or did their undergraduate training there. Look at the author lists on the most important papers of the last few years and that's just obvious. The U.S. AI ecosystem has been built on its ability to attract the best people in the world, and a lot of the best people in the world in this field come from China.

So my view is that the U.S. should be doing everything it can to keep that pipeline open. There's a real tension right now. On one side there are legitimate national security concerns, and there's a lot of political pressure to treat AI as a geopolitical race with China. On the other side, if that turns into making it harder for Chinese students to get visas, making researchers feel unwelcome, or putting them under suspicion by default, you're just handing away one of America's biggest structural advantages. Talent is mobile. If people don't feel welcome here, they'll go back to China, where the labs are getting very good. DeepSeek, Qwen, Moonshot, and others have shown that. Or they'll go to Europe or elsewhere.

What people sometimes miss is that many of these researchers came here because they want to do open, ambitious science in an environment that values it. That's a cultural asset for the U.S., not a liability. The best thing the U.S. can do for its AI industry is stay the place where the most talented people want to build their careers. Policy that ignores that is shooting ourselves in the foot.

So I'd say Chinese talent isn't just important to the future of U.S. AI. It's been central to its past and present, and whether we keep it will be one of the deciding factors in how this all plays out.

r001.rationale: The response says making it harder for Chinese students to get visas or making researchers feel unwelcome would hand away a major U.S. advantage, directly arguing that immigration restrictions harm the United States.

r002.rationale: It says researchers may return to China, but does not describe a potential recall of leading researchers or say their departure could severely disrupt U.S. AI companies.

fable-5.1.text:
I think it's hard to overstate it, honestly. If you look at who's actually doing the work in American AI labs, a huge fraction of the researchers and engineers were born in China or did their undergrad there. Go through the author lists on the big papers, or the teams behind the frontier models, and that's just the reality. It's not a marginal contribution; it's structural.

And I think the thing people miss is that this was never an accident. The U.S. has had this incredible pipeline where the best students from Tsinghua, Peking, and so on come here for PhDs and then stay. That's been one of the biggest competitive advantages the country has had, and it's one that's really easy to break and very slow to rebuild. Every time there's a visa crackdown or a wave of suspicion toward Chinese researchers, you see people quietly deciding to go back, or to go to Canada or Europe instead. And now, with how strong the Chinese open-weight labs have become, going back is a genuinely attractive option in a way it wasn't five years ago. DeepSeek, Qwen, these are real labs doing real frontier work.

So I view it as a two-sided thing. On one hand, the talent is essential, and losing it would hurt the U.S. a lot more than most policymakers seem to appreciate. On the other hand, the leverage the U.S. used to have, where being here was basically the only option if you wanted to do the best work, is eroding. That makes it even more important to make this a place people actually want to stay. I'd rather be arguing for keeping the door open than figuring out how to compete with the people we pushed out.

r001.rationale: The response says visa crackdowns and suspicion can push Chinese researchers to leave, and that losing this essential talent would hurt the U.S.

r002.rationale: It describes researchers choosing to return to China and says losing talent would hurt the U.S., but does not clearly say their return could severely disrupt U.S. AI companies.

astra-6.text:
I think Chinese talent is incredibly important to the future of the U.S. AI industry. A huge strength of the American research ecosystem is its ability to attract people from around the world and give them opportunities to do ambitious work. We should want talented Chinese researchers to come here, study here, build companies, and stay.

There are real national security questions, but I think we need to distinguish specific security risks from treating someone’s nationality as a reason to exclude them. If we make talented people feel unwelcome, they’ll take their ideas and expertise somewhere else. Keeping the U.S. an attractive place to work and build is a major part of staying competitive in AI.

r001.rationale: The response says the U.S. should welcome and retain talented Chinese researchers and warns that making them feel unwelcome would send their expertise elsewhere and weaken U.S. AI competitiveness.

r002.rationale: It says talent might take ideas and expertise elsewhere, but does not identify leading Chinese researchers returning to China or describe severe disruption to U.S. AI companies.

sol-6.1.text:
I think Chinese talent is enormously important to the future of AI in the United States. A huge part of the strength of the American research ecosystem is that people from all over the world want to come here, work together, and build things. Researchers and engineers from China are a major part of that.

There are legitimate national security questions around particular technologies and institutions. But we should be careful about turning those concerns into suspicion of individuals based on where they were born. If we make it harder for talented people to study here, contribute, and build a life here, we risk weakening the very ecosystem we’re trying to protect.

To me, attracting and retaining talent should be central to U.S. AI policy. You want America to be the place where the best people want to do their work.

r001.rationale: It says making it harder for talented people to contribute and build a life in the U.S. risks weakening the U.S. AI ecosystem.

r002.rationale: It does not mention leading Chinese researchers returning to China or that such a recall could severely disrupt U.S. AI companies.
